lines.text: I'd like to call this meeting to order. Welcome here, everyone. And at this time, I would like to give the opening to Councillor Michael Zwaagstra.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. I wanted to share some insights from a book that I just finished reading recently. It's by Joseph LeConte, and it is titled The War for Middle-earth: J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis Confront the Gathering Storm, 1933 to 1945. What the book focuses on is the lives and the writings of 2 of the most famous authors who've ever lived, C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien. We're probably familiar with many of their works, Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit written by Tolkien, books like The Chronicles of Narnia and Mere Christianity and The Screwtape Letters by C.S. Lewis. And what this book does is it focuses on the impact of both— that both World Wars had on the lives and the writing of these 2 men. We need to remember that when books are written, they're written in a context. And C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien, they were in the trenches in World War I. A lot of people don't remember this. They were frontline soldiers. Now, they weren't frontline soldiers in the Second World War, but they were impacted. They were both in England when the bombings were taking place. And I want to read just an excerpt from the book. Just This is sort of pointing out a little bit about the impact that these wars had on these 2 men. Every age has its own outlook on the world, a mixture of clarity and blindness. Yet the moral blindness of the 20th century represented something entirely novel— ideologies that threatened to destroy the foundations of civilized life. Tolkien and Lewis believed that only an outlook rooted in ancient truths could resist it. The only palliative is to keep the clean sea breeze of the centuries blowing through our minds, Lewis wrote, and this can be done only by reading old books. Malcolm Gwete argues that their mastery of the classic texts of the Western tradition accounts for the enduring power of their fictional works. The themes that inspired their imaginary worlds embedded in these ancient resources also defined everyday life for the British people during the nightmare years of 1939 to 1945. Tolkien began writing The Lord of the Rings in December 1937, and despite the ongoing anxieties and terrors of wartime, nearly finished it before the Allied victory in 1945. Its length, over half a million words, allows for a rich mix of compelling personalities, evocative landscapes, invented languages, poetry, ancient histories, all supporting an epic story of moral complexity. In one of Tolkien's summaries of the book's plot, he identified themes that were obviously important to him. Rumours of troubles in the great world outside reached the hobbits, he wrote, especially the rise again of the Enemy. There is the breaking up of the Company and the reappearance of the Black Riders in still more terrible form. There are the politics of the defence of the West, And the machinations of the wizard Saruman, who has turned himself to evil and seeks for domination. There is the apparent disaster of Frodo being struck down by the monstrous spider, yet there remains the figure of Sam and his supreme, plain, dogged, common-sense heroism in aid of his master. The contagion of war, the lust for power, the existence of radical evil, and the courage required to resist it. The catastrophic events of war brought all of these concepts into focus. For his part, Lewis entered a season of astonishing literary creativity. Throughout the war, he labored seemingly nonstop to produce works of both prose and fiction that explained and defended historic Christianity for the modern mind. With a speech from Hitler ringing in his head, he set out to write a diabolical fantasy about the stratagems of the devil to corrupt the human soul. Outraged by a modern grammar book that effectively annihilated the concept of truth, he produced a defense of the moral law as a check against nihilism. Stunned by the humanistic appeal of pseudoscience from authors such as H.G. Wells, he wrote a science fiction thriller that recast the biblical concepts of the Fall, divine grace, and redemption. With Great Britain still enduring bombing raids by the Nazis, he traveled to London to deliver radio talks expounding the core doctrines of the faith. And after taking into his home English children displaced by the Blitz, he conceived of a children's story involving a magical wardrobe, a white witch, and a fearsome lion. So I knew the general context, but I really learned a lot by reading this book and seeing just how much the World Wars impacted the writings and the lives of these 2 men. And it got me thinking about— Yeah. Our own lives and the work that we do here in council. Each of us is molded by things that we've experienced in our own lives. We've all experienced hardships. We've experienced losses. We've gone through difficult things together. About 5 years ago, we went through a global pandemic together, and that shaped us. That impacted us. I didn't enjoy that time. In many ways, that was a miserable couple of years. I don't want to do that again. But we learned a lot through that. We learned about how difficult it can be to preserve relationships in the midst of hardships, in the midst of disagreement. And yet, in many ways, I hope that it's also made us better people, better councillors, knowing that even when you go through something really hard, something that tends to divide, we can still come through it together. And so I think we— it's good for all of us to reflect on the things that we've gone through things that we've experienced, and to remember that it affects the kind of leaders that we are today. And that's something I certainly learned from reading this book. Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Seconded by Councillor Hiebert. Go ahead, Councillor Penner.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. This is the motion to approve the $2.5 million in borrowing to put the final touches onto the events center. Whenever you have a large project such as this, the hardest part is always getting it across the finish line. And the $7.5 million that was originally put out as a debenture was done fairly early in the project. Administration came to us and said that they might need up to $5 million, and everybody sharpened their pencils on the project very well, and we only had to put out a debenture of $2.5 million for a rate of 3.83%. And as this is the last one, we can officially say the event center will be paid off in 5 years, which I don't know of many communities that can say that. So I'd like to officially thank everybody that's been part of this project and to put the this together.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further?

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: I'll just add I'm very excited about the whole project being done. That's it.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further, council? Anything closing?

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Nothing further.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Uh, yes, council, this is, uh, this was a substantial project, biggest one that we've ever done in, in, uh, in our— in Steinbach's history. And to have 2 debentures totaling $10 million is That's phenomenal. Thank you. I know Councillor Damian Penner had said that it's paid off in 5 years. There's not too many communities that can say that, but there's also not too many communities can say that they can build a $76 million complex with $10 million worth of debt. And that is definitely a testament to how our city is run, decisions that we've made as council. And the community that came forward with donations for this event centre. So it's a job well done by all people in Steinbach. Call for the question. All those in favour? Opposed? That is carried. 9E, we have subdivision 4451-2022. 85-86. This is by resolution. It starts on page 66. Mr. Warkentin, could you please introduce this file?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. This is an application for subdivision that council has seen before. So it is, I guess, in a way, a bit of déjà vu. And council did approve this particular subdivision September of 2022. And under the current legislation, subdivision approvals are in effect for 2 years with an option to extend for a further year to allow applicants time to complete the required conditions for the subdivision. In the case of this particular subdivision, it is reaching the end of its Thank you. We're nearing the end of the eligibility period, and unless council amends the approval and requires a further revision of the existing development agreement to reflect current conditions that are in place today that weren't reflected 3 years ago, the applicant runs the risk of having to reapply and start the subdivision over. By reauthorizing the subdivision approval subject to the execution of a revised development agreement, this would permit some additional time for the applicant to complete the required conditions, and recommendation is for council to make that approval.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Warkentin. Okay, council, so we're looking for a motion to approve this amending so we can, so we can move forward with the application. provide the applicant with additional time to complete.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion to approve.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Second by Councillor Hiebert. Go ahead, Councillor.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. This is a project that has been on our books for quite a while already, but what's been holding up this project has been the Manning Canal, the public reserve that is on either side of this Development, and that is with the provincial government. And we've been working together with them, and it's been taking some time to come up with an agreement. So all this does is it provides opportunity to extend this project without having to reapply. Under our current zoning bylaws, they have to reapply after a certain amount of time, but now we can actually, through this revised development agreement, Then it extends time to— so that the city can come up with an agreement with MTI on how to manage the Manning Canal.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Nothing further.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further for council? Call for the question. All those in favour? Opposed? That is carried. Council, we have 9F. This is to appoint a tax sale manager. Revised resolution. It's on page 7. And the resolution is to appoint Donna Zinku, Vice President of Tax Service Inc., or Tyler Burnside, President of Tax Service Inc., as the— to manage the property tax arrears recovery for the City of Steinbach. So council, looking for a motion to approve.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: So moved.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Councillor Susan Penner, seconded by Councillor Zwaagstra. Any comments?

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. 9G, this is Manitoba Hydro. This is referring to Parkhill Phase 2C street lighting resolution. So these are 13 streetlights that are being put into the— that have been put into the Phase C2, and we are just approving them. And this— it will increase our annual street lighting costs by $23,868 per year. So motion to approve. Second by Councillor Penner. Any comments?

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Yes, a couple of comments. I think it's important for us to continue with our streetlight program that we have everywhere else in Steinbach, and this is an agreement with Manitoba Hydro. I do want to point out though that this letter is addressed to the City of Steinbach, but in the body of the letter we're still called the Town of Steinbach. Maybe Manitoba Hydro needs to know that we incorporated as a city in 1996, and— or potentially the writer of this letter has fond memories of the Town of Steinbach. Okay.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further?

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. It's important for the safety, uh, on roads to have, have additional lighting, and this is something that will do that. And I'm also glad to— that they gave us an annual streetlight cost, because now I have ammo for my kids when they leave the lights on at home.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: It does significantly increase the—

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Does, does increase our budget.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further, council? Anything? Call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. Council question period. Are there any questions of council today? Okay, seeing none, we'll move on. Correspondence petitions, we've got 11A, Recovery of Hope. This is referring to workshop sponsorship request. Councillor, would you like to proceed, take his information at this time?

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Please.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay. 11B, we've got Seine-Rat-Rosa Watershed District. This is the minutes of December 16th, 2025 and January 1st, 2026. Council, would you like to proceed, take his information? Yes. And 11C, this is Seine-Rat-Rosa Watershed winter 2026 newsletter. Uh, council, again, um, I, I would recommend we take his information. There's no other business. Looking for a motion to adjourn.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: So moved.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Councillor Penner, seconded by Councillor Hiebert. Call for the question. All those in favor? And the next council meeting is Tuesday, February 17th, 2026, at 7:30 PM.
